FREELANCE WRITER RATE CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Per-word rate or flat fee — which actually pays more per hour?

A per-word rate only pays for the words in the final piece. Research, interviews, outlining, and revision rounds are real hours the job costs you — and a pure per-word rate does not compensate any of them. This tool turns both pricing options into an effective hourly rate for the same job, so you can see which one actually pays more, not just which headline number looks bigger.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. The job

2. The two prices on offer

Leave the target hourly rate blank to skip the solver.

Fill in the job details and the two prices on offer, then click Calculate.

Result

What this does not cover

  • Not a rate card. This does not know your market, your niche, or a specific client's budget — it applies the hours and prices you enter to the job as you describe it.
  • Does not estimate your writing speed or research time for you. You supply both directly; a first draft of an unfamiliar topic routinely runs slower than a writer's own average.
  • No taxes, platform fees, or overhead. If you are also comparing what a job posted through Upwork or Fiverr nets after that platform's cut, see the Upwork vs. Fiverr fee calculator.
  • No client negotiation modeling. This does not predict whether a client will accept a higher flat fee instead of a per-word rate — it only compares the two prices you already have.

Common questions

Is a per-word rate or a flat project fee better for a freelance writer?

It depends on the job. A per-word rate only pays for words written -- it does not separately compensate research, interviews, outlining, or revision rounds. A flat fee prices the whole job, including that non-writing time. When a job has heavy research or several revision rounds, a flat fee usually pays a higher effective hourly rate than an equivalent per-word rate; when a job is fast to write with little revision, a good per-word rate can pay more per hour.

What counts as a low per-word rate in 2026?

2026 freelance rate surveys put entry-level content writing at roughly $0.05-$0.10 per word, intermediate-to-senior generalist work at $0.10-$0.50 per word, and specialist work (legal, medical, expert B2B/fintech) at $0.50-$2.00+ per word. A 500-writer survey put the across-the-board average at $0.42/word; a survey of established copywriters put their average at $0.70/word -- the two differ because they sample different populations, not because either is wrong.

Do ghostwriters charge more than bylined writers?

Most freelance writers do not charge extra for ghostwriting (no byline). Of the writers who do add a premium, most add 16-20% over their bylined rate for the same word count, per 2026 rate-guide surveys. This tool shows that range as information only -- it is never added to the numbers automatically.

Why does research and revision time matter to the price?

A per-word rate is calculated only against the words in the final piece. If a job needs four hours of research and two revision rounds before the words are final, that time still has to be paid for somehow -- and a pure per-word rate does not do it. Rate guides describe switching from per-word to flat per-project pricing as the single most reliable way an established writer raises their real income, without ever raising the per-word figure they quote.

Is this a rate card or a guarantee of what to charge?

No. This tool applies the hours and prices you enter to compute an effective hourly rate for the job as you describe it -- it does not know your market, your niche, or your client's budget, and it is not a substitute for your own judgment or a professional rate-card resource.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not financial, legal, or professional advice, and it does not replace your own judgment about your market or a client's budget. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (estimate_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Pricing a one-off job instead of an ongoing retainer? The freelance retainer calculator compares a monthly retainer against hourly billing for recurring client work — nothing uploaded. Comparing what the same job nets on Upwork vs. Fiverr after platform fees? See the Upwork vs. Fiverr fee calculator.

Quoting an editing or proofreading job instead of writing? The freelance editor quote calculator turns word count, edit level and your hourly target into a flat fee and per-word rate.

This calculator vs. judging a quote by its headline number

$0.20/word and $500 flat both sound like reasonable prices for one article. Neither number says how many hours the job actually takes — and this calculator's own worked example shows what dividing by those hours does to both of them.

Two respectable-looking numbers, one worked example

Judged by the headline number aloneDivided by this job's actual 9 hours
$0.20/word is above the 2026 entry-level floor of $0.10/word — looks like a fair per-word rate.$300 total ÷ 9 hours = $33.33/hr.
$500 for one article sounds like solid, above-average pay.$500 ÷ 9 hours = $55.56/hr.
Both numbers look acceptable on their own, and neither mentions an hourly figure at all.A $22.22/hr gap between them, and both fall short of a $75/hr target.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

The same job, worked through this calculator

Take this calculator's own example: a 1,500-word article, written at 500 words an hour, with 4 hours of research and two one-hour revision rounds — 9 total hours. Offered $0.20/word, that's $300. Offered a $500 flat fee instead, that's more money outright, and both numbers individually clear most writers' sense of "that sounds fine."

Neither number says what it pays per hour. Divide each by the same 9 hours the job actually takes and the per-word rate comes to $33.33/hr, the flat fee to $55.56/hr — a $22.22/hr gap that was invisible from either headline price on its own, and both short of a $75/hr target this worked example checks against. Reaching that target on this same job would take a $0.45/word rate or a $675 flat fee, not the $0.20 or $500 either quote actually offered.

Common questions

What's wrong with judging a quote by whether the number sounds reasonable?

A headline price and an hourly rate are different questions, and a headline number that clears your own mental bar for "seems fair" can still pay far less per hour than you'd accept if it were phrased as an hourly rate. $0.20/word is above the 2026 entry-level floor of $0.10/word, and $500 for one article sounds like solid pay -- neither number says anything about how many hours the job actually takes to reach that word count.

Why does dividing by hours change the answer?

Because a headline price is a single number and an hourly rate is that number divided by every hour the job costs, including hours a per-word rate does not separately pay for: research, interviews, outlining, and revision rounds. Two prices that look similar side by side, or that both individually sound acceptable, can turn out to differ by tens of dollars an hour once the same total hours are divided into each -- a gap invisible from either headline number alone.

What does this calculator's own worked example show?

A 1,500-word article at 500 words/hour, with 4 hours of research and two one-hour revision rounds, comes to 9 total hours. A $0.20/word rate ($300 total) and a $500 flat fee both look like reasonable, similar-enough numbers for one article. Divided by those 9 hours, they are $33.33/hr and $55.56/hr -- a $22.22/hr gap, and both under a $75/hr target that neither headline number hinted at.

Isn't a bigger headline number always the better deal?

For the SAME job, yes -- the higher total dollar amount and the higher effective hourly rate always agree, because both prices are being divided by the identical total hours. What the headline number can't tell you is what that hourly rate actually IS, or whether it clears a target you have in mind. A $500 fee sounds bigger than $300, but only the hourly figure tells you it still falls short of $75/hr.

Does this calculator know how many hours my job will really take?

No. You supply the word count, your writing speed, research hours, and revision rounds; the calculator turns those into a total and divides each price by it. It does not estimate your speed or a client's revision demands for you -- see "What this does not cover" on the calculator page.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply the hours and prices you enter to compute an effective hourly rate.
